client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back. I mean that — last week felt hard, and here you are again. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I... I almost didn't. Sat in my car for like twenty minutes, honestly. I kept telling myself I was just doing it to get Sara off my back. She's been calling every day since the, um, the intervention thing, which — I don't even love that word for it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of it was for Sara. And part of you drove here anyway.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean. Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: How has this past week been? You mentioned last time you were in the middle of a piece.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I painted. I mean, I've been working. Had wine while I worked, which — that's just how I work, okay? That's how I've always worked. I'm not going to apologize for it. Half the artists people worship were drunk half the time. It's part of the process, it's not some big red flag.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking has been part of how you make things — woven right into the process, for a long time.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. It... it does something. Or it did, I think. It used to feel like it opened a door between my brain and my hand, like I could stop picking everything apart and just let it come out. I don't know, lately I'm not... I'm not sure it's doing that the same way. But I'm still making things, so.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're still making things. What does what you're making feel like lately, to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Like... not mine, kind of? It looks like my work technically, like you'd know it was me. But it's — it's coming from somewhere flat. I've actually been really productive, which is the thing nobody understands. I'm producing a lot. It just doesn't feel like me inside it anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can see yourself in it from the outside. But something essential — something that makes it yours — isn't there when you're in it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And I keep... I keep opening a bottle thinking that's what'll bring it back. Like if I just find the right amount, the right moment. But I'm putting out more work than ever and none of it means anything to me. How does that happen? How do you make more and feel less?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've kept reaching for the thing that used to work. And it's not giving you back what it once did.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. And I think — okay. I think I've been using it as like, proof. 'I drink, therefore I'm a real artist.' That whole thing. But if the drinking is supposed to unlock all this great work and the work is getting worse... then either I'm wrong about myself as an artist, or I've been wrong about what the alcohol is actually doing. And I don't know which one scares me more.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to sit with. What feels true to you right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Both feel terrifying. But I think... I think somewhere I've known for a while that the alcohol isn't what makes the art. I think it just... gave me something to hide behind. In case the art was never good to begin with. And now I'm scared to find out what's actually there — or not there — without it.

client_context: A 40-year-old single parent who has been drinking a bottle of wine nightly to cope with the stress of raising two kids alone. Knows it's too much but feels trapped.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm really glad you came back in today. I know last week was... a lot. How are you feeling coming into this session?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I don't really want to be here. My sister basically dragged me back, so... yeah. I had a hard week, okay? That doesn't mean I have some kind of problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you're frustrated — maybe feeling like you're here because someone else wanted you to be, not really for yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. She calls my mom, my mom calls me, and suddenly I'm the one with the problem. I'm the one working two jobs and raising two kids by myself. They don't live my life. They have no idea what my days look like.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two jobs. Two kids. All on your own. That's... that's a tremendous amount to carry.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And nobody helps. Like, ever. My sister actually called me an alcoholic. Me. I have a glass of wine — okay, a couple glasses — to unwind at night. That is what adults do. That is normal. I wait until the kids are asleep, I'm not drinking at work, I'm not... I don't know why everyone's acting like I'm some kind of disaster.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one side, there's your family calling and worrying. And on the other side, there's you — holding everything together, and the wine at the end of the day is what lets you finally breathe.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean — look, last week was really bad. I know I drank more than usual. I'm not saying I didn't. I just... it was a bad week. That's all it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It means something that you said that — that you know it went further than usual. That wasn't easy to say. What happened last week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My son — he's nine — he got in trouble at school. And I just... I completely lost it on him. Like, really yelled. And he started crying and I just stood there and I... I ended up drinking almost two bottles that night just to like, stop feeling so terrible about it. Which I know, I know how that sounds.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're still carrying that. What happened with him.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He's a good kid. He's just... he's having a hard time too. His dad's not in the picture and I think he's acting out because of that and I just... I took it out on him instead of, I don't know. Being his mom.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Even in that moment — even when you were at your worst — you noticed what he needed. You saw him. That's still you being his mom, even when it's really hard.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want the wine to be the thing, you know? Like, the thing that gets me through. That's not... that's not who I want to be. I just genuinely don't know how else to turn my brain off at the end of the day. It's the only time I get to just... stop.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm hearing you. You've had a brutal week — two jobs, everything with your son, all of it on your own. And part of you knows the drinking went further than you're comfortable with. And another part of you is starting to wonder if there's a different way to find that quiet at the end of the day. Does that feel right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's pretty much it. I don't know what that looks like yet. But yeah.

client_context: A 38-year-old mandated by court to attend counseling after a second DUI. Furious about being forced to be here. Sees the system as unfair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, grab whatever seat's comfortable. And I'll be upfront with you right now — I'm not here to lecture you, I'm not here to tell you what you did wrong. You've probably had enough of that from everyone else lately.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, you could say that. Look, I'll be straight with you too — I don't want to be here. No offense. I'm here because a judge decided that's what happens now, and if I don't show, I lose my license permanently. So. Here I am. Doing this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The whole thing feels like it's being done to you. Like you didn't get a say in any of it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Because I didn't! Two miles from my buddy's place — two miles. I know that road, I've driven it a hundred times, nobody got hurt, nobody was even out there. And now I've blown through detox, I'm paying God knows what for these sessions, and my ex-wife is using every single bit of it against me in the custody hearing. So yeah. I'm a little — yeah. I'm a little pissed off.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're carrying a lot right now. The legal stuff, the custody battle, all of it landing at once — and you still walked in here today. That's not a small thing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I didn't exactly have a choice. But. Yeah. I'm here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned detox — you just came out of that. What was that experience actually like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It was... I don't know. Humiliating, honestly. I'm 38 years old, I managed a team of twelve people — twelve — and I'm sitting in there like... I'm not judging anybody else who was there, that's not what I mean, but I just kept thinking, this isn't me. This is not who I am. I don't belong here. That's all I could think the whole time.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you say 'this isn't me' — I'm curious what you mean by that. Who is the version of you that's supposed to be there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Someone who... has it together. My dad was a drinker — like, a real drinker — and I spent my whole childhood swearing I'd never be that guy. Never. And then last month the doctor calls me in, starts talking about liver enzymes, elevated this, we need to monitor that, and I'm sitting across from him thinking... when did this happen. Like, when exactly did this become my life. Because I wasn't — I wasn't trying to be him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That call from the doctor landed differently than everything else. The judge, the cop, the custody stuff — all of that you can push back on, argue with, be angry at. But the lab results are harder to fight.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's actually exactly right. I've been furious at the judge, furious at the cop who pulled me over, at my ex. But you can't — you can't argue with a blood test. It's just... numbers. And I sat in my car for like an hour after that appointment. Just sat there in the parking lot. Didn't go anywhere. Just sat.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was going through your mind, sitting in that car?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My kids. I've got two — eight and eleven. And I kept thinking... what's the version of this where they're okay. Where I'm actually there for them. Not just physically there, like showing up, I mean really there. Present. And um... I don't think I've been that. Not lately. Maybe not for a while, if I'm being honest with myself.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because there's a lot here. There's still real anger about how all this went down — and that part doesn't feel unfair for no reason, some of it genuinely wasn't in your control. But then there's a phone call from a doctor, and an hour alone in a parking lot, and it keeps coming back to the same place — your kids, and who you want to be for them. That thread seems important.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. I mean — I'm still pissed about the court stuff, I'm not gonna sit here and pretend I'm not. But... yeah. There's something to figure out here. I don't know what that looks like yet or where to even start, but... maybe this isn't a total waste of time. Maybe.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, Margaret. Good to see you made it in — I know last week sounded rough on the phone. So, catch me up. How've things been since we talked?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, you know... not great. I had a — well, I'd call it a bad few days. The pain flared up something awful Tuesday night and I... I made some choices I'm not proud of.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Choices you're not proud of. You're leading with that — not burying it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I took more of the Vicodin, and then I had... three, maybe four glasses of wine on top of it. Told myself it would just take the edge off. But I fell asleep in the recliner and my daughter Carol found me and she was — she was frightened. Really frightened.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That sounds like a scary moment for both of you. What was it like waking up to that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Embarrassing. And then I got defensive with her, which I shouldn't have done. She was worried and I snapped at her. I felt... cornered. Like she was making a fuss over nothing. Except... it wasn't nothing, was it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're already asking yourself that question. Whether it was nothing. That's not a small thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I've been thinking about it all week. I keep telling myself I have it under control — that at my age, with the hip and the back, I've... I don't know, earned a little relief. But the look on Carol's face. She was terrified. And I don't want to be someone who terrifies their children.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is saying: I've been managing a lot of real pain for a long time, and this is just how I cope. And then there's Carol's face saying something else entirely. What do you make of that gap?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's the thing, isn't it. I've been telling myself I'm not burdening anyone because I'm handling it myself. But if handling it myself means my daughter shows up at 11 o'clock at night thinking I'm... that I'm dead in a recliner — that's not not burdening her. That's the opposite of that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a sharp piece of thinking right there. You've spent years trying to protect everyone from your pain — and it found a way to scare them anyway. Funny how that works. Not ha-ha funny.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No, not ha-ha funny. *laughs a little* My late husband used to say I was stubborn as a fence post. He wasn't wrong. But maybe... maybe this time stubborn isn't actually protecting anyone. Including me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it actually look like — to let someone help for once?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think I'd have to really talk to Carol. Not brush her off, actually talk. And... I've been avoiding telling Dr. Patel the whole picture because I didn't want him thinking I'm some kind of — I don't know, a drug seeker or something. But the way things are going, I'm not managing the pain anymore. The pain is managing me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull this together, if that's okay. You came in today and named what happened — the mixing, falling asleep, Carol's fear. You could've softened all of that and you didn't. You figured out, on your own, that protecting people from your pain was actually causing them more worry, not less. And now you're talking about a real conversation with Carol and being honest with Dr. Patel. That's not a small shift. That's actually a big one.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is, isn't it. I think I've been scared. Of being a burden but also of... admitting I can't do this alone anymore. I'm 72, not 35. Maybe it's alright to need a little help.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You came back. I just want to say that... that means something. Last week felt heavy, and you still showed up today. How are you doing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well. Margaret said I had to. Or... I don't know. Maybe I wanted to. Hard to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Part of you wanted to be here.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess so. It's just... the week was the same as always. Had a couple drinks in the evening. Margaret didn't say anything but she gave me that look, you know? I've been getting that look a lot lately.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That look carries a lot of weight. I'm curious about something — what did your days feel like before you retired? Like, what did a Tuesday morning feel like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh... different. Completely different. I was regional manager for twenty-two years. I mean, the phone didn't stop. People needed decisions, they needed... they needed me to show up. And I did. Every day. That was just... that's who I was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: People needed you. You had a place, a reason to get up. And then retirement came, and... what happened to that man?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He... I don't know. He just kind of... I wake up at seven out of habit and then I just sit there. The house is quiet. Margaret has her book club and her friends, and that's good, I'm glad she has that, but I'm just... I'm sitting there and it's like, what am I for now? And the drinking, it um... it fills the time. It makes the quiet less loud, if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The quiet is loud. That's a painful thing to sit with every morning. And the drinking has been a way to soften that... that emptiness.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. I never thought of myself as someone who... I mean, I had a glass of wine at dinner like anybody else. But now it's more than that and I know it's more than that. I'm not stupid. The doctor said my liver numbers are off and I thought, well, that's... that scared me a little. More than a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You heard that and something shifted. What did you think about in those days after the doctor's appointment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I thought about my father. He died at sixty-eight. And I thought... I don't want to go like that. I've got grandkids, three of them, and they're little. Charlie's only four. I want to be there, you know? I want to be the grandfather who... who actually shows up. Not the one they have to tiptoe around.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to hold all of that for a moment. You spent twenty-two years being someone who showed up, who people counted on. Retirement took that from you, and in that emptiness, drinking became a way to quiet the noise of not knowing who you are anymore. But sitting here today, what I'm also hearing is a man who loves his grandchildren, who doesn't want to repeat his father's story, and who deep down knows this isn't who he wants to be. And you came back here. That tells me something about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
...

When you say it like that... I don't know, it sounds like something I could actually... like maybe it's not too late. Margaret hasn't left. The kids still call. I've been waiting for everything to fall apart and it hasn't yet. Maybe I've been just waiting to hit bottom instead of just... stopping before I get there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to wait for the bottom. You get to choose where the floor is. If you were to take one small step this week — just one — toward being that grandfather, that husband, that man you're describing... what might that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe I call my son. Ask if I can take Charlie to the park Saturday. Just... be somewhere I'm supposed to be. And maybe I pour one drink instead of three. I'm not saying I can do it all at once but... yeah. Yeah, I think I want to try.

client_context: A 29-year-old who moved to a new country alone and started drinking to cope with loneliness and cultural adjustment. Has no local support system.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's really good to see you again. I know the last few weeks have been... a lot. How have things been since we spoke?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I didn't really want to come today, if I'm being honest. My sister called my mom, my mom called me, and then it was this whole... thing. So. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like you're feeling a bit pushed into being here. Like the choice wasn't really yours.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Because everyone back home is just — they're panicking, okay? Like they think I'm some kind of... I don't know. They don't understand what it's like here. They have never lived somewhere alone where nobody knows your name. Not one of them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What is it like here... for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's just... work, go home, work, go home. I told you last time things were getting better and then — they weren't. There was this rough patch and I hate that I have to sit here and talk about it because it just makes me feel stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The progress you'd made — it felt like it slipped away somehow. And now you're sitting with that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: There was this team lunch at work. And I just... I couldn't make myself go. I stood outside the restaurant for like ten minutes and then I just walked home. And I drank most of a bottle of wine by myself and I cried. And I felt so, so stupid.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took real courage to share just now. That moment sounds incredibly painful — being right there, wanting to walk in, and something just... stopping you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Why is it so hard? Back home I had people. I could call someone at midnight and they'd just come over, no questions. Here I don't even have... I don't have anyone's number. Like, a real friend. Not one.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the loneliness is still there underneath everything. And when a moment like that lunch comes along — a real chance to connect — something pulls you back. And then the wine becomes the way to get through the night.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. When you say it like that it sounds — I don't know. It sounds sad. It is sad.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You had those deep friendships back home. I'm curious — what do you think made it possible to have that kind of closeness with people?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: We just... grew up together. We had history already. Here I have to start from nothing and I'm already 29 and everyone already has their lives and their friends and... I don't know where to even begin. But I know I don't want to feel like this forever. I do know that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something in you knows this isn't where you want to stay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. It's not. I moved here for a reason. I wanted something different. I just got so caught up in how hard it was that I forgot what I actually came here for. I think... I think I need to actually try. Like really try to meet people. Maybe that lunch was a sign. I don't know.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you came in. I know you mentioned the ER when you called to reschedule. Before we get into anything else — how are you doing right now, just sitting here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm fine. I mean — look, I don't really need to be here, that's the honest truth. The whole ER thing got blown way out of proportion. I had too much to drink, my wife panicked, called 911. She does that. It wasn't... I wasn't in danger or anything. I've seen guys actually hurt. This wasn't that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: From your perspective, she made it into something much bigger than what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I wasn't dying. I've had way worse nights and been fine. But she freaked out and now I'm sitting here. That's just — that's how it goes. I end up in some office talking about my feelings and she gets to feel like she did something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What's been happening at home since the hospital?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She's at her sister's. Took the kids. She said... um... she said if I just come in here and go through the motions again, she's filing. So. I don't even know why I'm telling you that right now. It's — I just need her to calm down and come home and things go back to normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You showed up anyway. With your wife gone, the kids gone, all that weight — you still walked through that door today. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I didn't have much of a choice, right? But look — I'm not gonna sit here and say I'm an alcoholic or whatever. I drink. Okay. It helps me sleep, it quiets the noise. I've been doing this since I got back and I'm functional, I go to work, I'm not — it's not like I'm some homeless guy under a bridge. I can handle it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned she took the kids. When that actually happened — when they walked out — what was going on inside you in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... I just kind of stood there. It was like getting hit and not being able to fall, you know? And I don't — I know I haven't been great lately. I'm there but I'm not there. My oldest, Marcus, he's nine. He used to ask me every weekend to throw the ball around. And I didn't even — I didn't notice he stopped asking. She had to tell me. That's... that's pretty messed up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: He stopped asking, and somewhere along the way you stopped noticing he had.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah that's — that's exactly right. And I don't want that. I didn't come back from two deployments to be a ghost in my own house. That's not... that's not who I am. Or it's not who I was. I don't know what I am anymore, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to reflect back what I'm hearing, and stop me if I get it wrong. You came in after a really brutal week — the ER, your wife and kids leaving. One part of you is still saying this isn't a real problem, that the drinking is something you manage, that you're functional. And there's another part that noticed something this week — your son stopped asking for you, and you weren't even there enough to catch it. You made it through two deployments, and now you're standing in your own living room feeling like a ghost.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. When you say it out loud like that it sounds — I don't know. It's different. I always thought I'd come home and just... decompress. Be okay. Get back to normal. And I've been waiting to feel okay for like four years now and I'm still just... waiting. I'm still waiting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Four years of waiting to feel okay. What would it look like — even just a little bit — if things started moving in a different direction for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe... maybe I'm actually there when Marcus asks me something. Maybe Sarah doesn't look at me like she's already grieving. I don't know how to get there, I really don't. But I — I think I want to try. I think. That's something, right?

client_context: A 34-year-old artist who believes alcohol fuels creativity. Has been drinking daily for years. Recently noticed the art has gotten worse, not better.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey — you came back. I'll be honest, I wasn't a hundred percent sure you would. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well... my sister wouldn't stop texting me, so. Here I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ha — I'll have to send her a thank-you card. So, last time we barely scratched the surface. What's been on your mind since then, if anything?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... honestly? I've been thinking about what you said about the drinking. But I keep coming back to the same thing — like, I genuinely believe it helps me create. I've done my best work when I'm... not fully sober. That's just true for me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the alcohol feels like it's part of the process — like it opens a door that's otherwise stuck.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. It's like... the inner critic just shuts up, you know? And I can go. But lately... I don't know. The stuff I've been making feels off. Like, technically it's fine, but there's no life in it. I keep staring at my canvases thinking, who painted this?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The work feels like it belongs to someone else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. And here's the thing that's messing with me — I've been drinking more than I used to. Not less. And the art is worse. So if alcohol is supposed to be the thing that helps... why is that happening? That doesn't track.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to notice. Can I share something with you — there's actually some interesting research on exactly that question, the alcohol-creativity connection. Would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Sure.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So what the research actually shows is that alcohol does lower inhibitions short-term — and that can feel like freedom, like the critic went quiet. But it simultaneously suppresses the prefrontal cortex, which is where complex creative connections actually get made. The nuance, the depth, the thing that makes a piece feel alive. And over time, with heavier use, that capacity starts to erode. The myth that alcohol fuels creativity is pretty well debunked. What it's really doing is muting the critic — but it's also muting the artist.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...huh. It's muting the artist. I've never heard it put that way. I always thought of the drinking as like... a tool. A feature, not a bug. But if it's taking away more than it's giving... God. That's a lot to sit with.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing. You came back today — which wasn't nothing. You've carried this belief for years that alcohol is part of who you are as an artist, and that belief has been real and meaningful to you. And at the same time, you're noticing the work has gotten flatter, and you're drinking more, not less — and you're not willing to just wave that away. There's a version of you in here who wants her art back.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's — that's it exactly. I want my art back. I've been telling myself this is about the drinking but it's always been about the art. That's the thing I actually care about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That feels important. So if the art is what's at the center of this for you — what feels like even a small possible step that might give your actual artist a little more room to show up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... maybe I try painting sober. Like, just once. Just to see what comes out. I'm kind of terrified to, honestly. But maybe that's the point.

client_context: A 50-year-old who was sober for 3 years but relapsed after a sudden job loss. Feels deep shame and hopelessness. Has been to AA before.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I know you just finished detox a few days ago — that's not nothing. I'm glad you came in. What's it like being here today, sitting across from me?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's... I don't know. Embarrassing. I had three years. Three years sober, and I just — I blew it. My daughter basically had to drag me here and I feel like a goddamn failure sitting in this chair again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Three years of your life — and now you're back at square one, and that feels like proof that you failed.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... the detox itself wasn't bad. I've been through worse, so. It's just — being here again. I thought I was past this kind of thing. I really did.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about the job. What did that actually do to you when it happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you think it did? I was there eighteen years. Eighteen. They handed me a box on a Tuesday morning and that was it. And I wasn't even — I mean I was sober, I was doing everything right, and it still didn't matter. So yeah. I had a drink. What was I supposed to do, just sit there?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were doing everything right — and it still fell apart anyway. That's a real loss, not just the paycheck. Your whole routine, your identity, the ground under your feet. And you reached for the one thing that used to quiet that feeling.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. That's — yeah, that's exactly it. I didn't plan it. I wasn't sitting there going 'I'm gonna drink tonight.' I just... it was there. And then it wasn't a few drinks anymore, it went sideways pretty fast. Faster than I remembered.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned three years. When things were actually working — what was holding you up back then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: AA, mostly. My sponsor Jim — I was calling him every week, sometimes more. And I had the job, I had somewhere to be every morning. I was... I actually felt like a person, you know? Not just some guy with a problem. Like I was building something for once.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You built something real. Three years isn't luck — that's you making a hard choice, over and over, every single day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I know. I do know that. I just — when everything went sideways I stopped calling Jim. I pulled away from everyone. That was... that was my mistake. I can see that pretty clearly now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull this together. You walked in here today ashamed, feeling like you threw everything away. And at the same time, you're telling me — you know what worked. You know what you stopped doing. The calls to Jim, the structure, feeling like you were building toward something. You haven't forgotten how to do this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, I haven't. And my daughter — she showed up. Even after all of this, she still showed up. I can't keep doing this to her. I don't want to.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: With all of that on the table — the shame, what you've learned about yourself, your daughter showing up — where does that leave you right now? What do you want to do with this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to call Jim. Today, actually — not tomorrow. And I think... I think I need more than just AA this time. I need to actually talk to somebody. Like, regularly. I don't want to white-knuckle it again and pretend I'm fine.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus. I know you didn't exactly sign up for this call. Before we get into anything — what's it like for you right now, being here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's fine. Whatever. My parents are being dramatic about the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: They're blowing this way out of proportion.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly. Like I had some beers, okay? It's not like — I don't know, everybody does it. My friends all drink. I'm not some like... alcoholic or whatever they think I am.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you think your parents are actually afraid of?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't— ...I mean, I guess they think I have some kind of problem. Which I don't. They found a few bottles in my room and now it's like this whole... thing. My mom literally cried. Over nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You said 'over nothing' — but you also mentioned your mom cried. That landed somewhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah, okay, that sucked. But that's not — like, she's making it about her. I'm the one who's... whatever. Forget it. It's complicated.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's complicated. I hear that. Can you help me understand what drinking actually does for you — like when you reach for it, what's going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's like... everything just gets quieter. My parents are always fighting, school is a lot right now, and I just — I go to my room and it's still loud, you know? In my head. And it helps with that. I know that probably sounds like an excuse.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's not an excuse. That's you trying to survive something that genuinely sounds exhausting. Sixteen years old, carrying all of that noise by yourself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. And now I've just made everything worse. Like my dad won't even look at me. Which is — I don't know, that's its own thing. And my mom keeps asking if I'm okay but in that way where she's not actually asking, she's just scared, and I... yeah. I don't know. I messed up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull together what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. Things at home have been really hard for a while — the fighting, the tension — and your head doesn't give you much quiet. Drinking became the thing that helped with that. But now the way it came out, it's added more pain on top of what was already there. And I think underneath the 'whatever, it's fine' from earlier... there's someone who's actually pretty scared right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...I didn't think it would turn into this. I thought I was just handling stuff. Like, quietly, on my own, no big deal. And then... I don't know. Maybe I wasn't handling it that well. Maybe I was just hiding it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That right there — that's real honesty. You came into this call ready to tell me everything was fine, and you're still here, actually talking. That matters. So let me ask you this: if things genuinely got better — not perfect, just better — what would that even look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... I want my mom to stop looking at me like I broke something. And I want to — I don't know, not feel like I need to do that just to get through a week. I'm kind of just really tired. Like, tired tired. And I think maybe I need to actually talk to someone for real. Not just sit in my room.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know this is your first session after finishing detox, and I imagine that's a lot to hold. What's it like being here right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? It's... weird. I kept telling myself I'd be relieved once detox was done, like, okay, check that box. But I'm sitting here and I just feel kind of exposed, I guess. Like the thing I used to get through the day isn't there anymore and now I have to figure out what comes next. Which is terrifying but also—I don't know—maybe good? I think I'm ready to actually deal with this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You finished something really hard, and instead of running from what comes next, you showed up. That tells me a lot about who you are.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I had to. My doctor basically told me I didn't have a choice, so—it wasn't exactly like I just decided one day. And I don't know if I'm actually ready or if I'm just saying I am because that's what I'm supposed to say in here. Um. Sorry. That sounds worse than I meant it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: No, don't apologize—that's exactly the kind of honest I want in here. It sounds like part of you isn't sure this was really your call. What would you say it was for you, though, underneath the referral?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, look—I'm an ER nurse. I have seen things that would make most people's brains break. Like legitimately traumatic things, every single shift, for two years straight during COVID. And drinking was just... it was a way to turn the volume down, you know? It's not like I have some disease or I was drinking at work or whatever. It was after hours. I was coping. Everyone copes somehow.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were doing the only thing that felt like it worked after carrying all of that. And for a while, it did work—it turned the volume down. Something shifted at some point, though.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, well—I don't know when exactly. It just... crept up. Stopped being a glass of wine after a bad shift and became like, I need this or I can't sleep, I can't eat, I can't think straight. And then I started showing up to work feeling like absolute garbage and—god, I was so foggy. I caught myself almost making a med error in November and I just... that scared me. Really scared me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A near-miss with a patient. That's not a small thing to carry. What was going through your head in that moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I thought... I thought, what if I had actually done it. What if I hurt someone. I got into nursing because I wanted to help people and I was—I was becoming a liability. The person I was at the start of my career, she would be horrified by where I ended up. I just kept thinking about all the times I told myself it was fine and it wasn't fine and I... I don't know. I let it go too far.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The nurse you set out to be still matters deeply to you. Enough that when she was at risk, it cut right through everything else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... Yeah. I haven't said that out loud before. It's—it's embarrassing, you know? Like I'm supposed to be the one who keeps it together. That's literally my job. And I couldn't even keep it together for myself. I think I'm just really sad about who I was for the last couple of years. I don't want to be that person anymore.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I've heard so far, see if I've got it right. You came into nursing with a real sense of purpose—to help people, to hold steady when everything's falling apart. The pandemic took an enormous toll, and drinking became the only relief valve you had. Over time, it stopped being something you chose and started running the show. Then November happened, and something in you said: this is not who I am. You went through detox. You're here. And underneath the fear and the grief about these last couple of years, I'm hearing someone who still really cares about getting back to herself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's—yeah. That's it exactly. I do want to get back to her. I miss her. I know that sounds dumb, like, missing yourself, but I do. And I think... I think I actually believe I can. Like maybe for the first time in a while I actually think this could work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That belief matters—hold onto it. What does getting back to her look like in the next few months, in a way that feels real and not just something you're supposed to say?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... staying sober, obviously, but more than that—going back to work and actually feeling present. Not white-knuckling through shifts. I want to feel like I'm good at what I do again, not just surviving it. And sleep. Like actual real sleep, not just passing out. I don't need everything figured out today, but I want to start building something. I feel like today was a start.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm glad you reached out. I know these first conversations can feel a little strange, especially over a screen. So... what's going on for you right now? What made today the day you called?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? My wife basically gave me an ultimatum. So, I mean... here I am. I'm not sure I even think there's like a real problem, but she does, so. I figured I'd at least show up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So part of you is here because you love her and you don't want to lose her... and another part of you is sitting there thinking 'I don't even know why I'm doing this.'

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... pretty accurate. Like I bartend, right? I've been doing it since I was twenty-two. Drinking after a shift is just — that's just what you do. Every single person I work with does the same thing. It's how you decompress. It's how you like, turn your brain off after being on your feet for eight hours with drunk people yelling at you. It's not — I don't know, it doesn't feel like a problem to me, it just feels like my life.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's woven into everything — the job, the culture, the way you unwind. It makes complete sense that it wouldn't feel like a problem from the inside. I'm curious... when your wife brought this up, what did she actually say to you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said she feels like she doesn't even know me anymore. Like I come home and I'm already halfway gone and we don't — we don't really talk. And I just... I got so pissed when she said that. Because I'm working, you know? I'm working hard for us. And I come home and instead of getting like, I don't know, any kind of warmth, I get this speech about how I'm checked out and... it feels like nothing I do is ever enough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: There's so much in that. The exhaustion of working hard and still feeling like you're falling short... that's a really painful place to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. Yeah it is. And like — okay, I'll be honest. I was sitting there the other night and I was trying to think of... when was the last time I didn't drink. And I couldn't. I literally could not think of a single day in, like, months. Maybe longer. And that kind of freaked me out a little. Not a lot. But a little.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment... when you couldn't find that day. What was that like, sitting with that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Weird. It was just weird. Like I kept going back further and further and I couldn't find it and I thought, okay, that's — is that normal? I genuinely don't know anymore if that's normal. My dad drank every day and nobody ever said anything about it, so I just always assumed... I don't know. I don't know what I assumed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You learned what normal looked like from him. And now you're in this moment where you're genuinely asking — for maybe the first time — whether the map you were given was the right one. That takes courage to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never really thought about it like that. My dad was just... he was a good guy. He worked hard. He drank. That was him. And I always said I was nothing like him, but... I mean. I work hard. I drink. That is me. Right now, that is me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If you could design what your life looked like a year from now — with your wife, with how you feel when you wake up in the morning — what would you want that to look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd want her to still be there. That's the first thing. And I'd want to actually... remember the conversations we have. Because there have been nights where she tells me something and I'll find out later I just don't have it. It's gone. And I hate that. I hate that I do that to her. I don't want to be that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to reflect back what I've heard today, because I think you've said something really significant. You came in thinking you might not have a problem. And somewhere in this conversation you found yourself wondering when you last had a sober day, recognizing a pattern you learned from your father, and telling me that you don't want to be someone who disappears on the person he loves. You haven't committed to anything today, and that's okay. But something in you is paying attention. And that matters.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I think something in me has been paying attention for a while. I just didn't really want to look at it. Maybe I'm ready to look at it a little.

client_context: A 31-year-old new mother who has been drinking wine nightly since the baby was born to cope with postpartum stress. Partner is supportive but worried.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for making time today — I know carving out an hour with a new baby at home is no small thing. Before we get into anything, I just want you to know this is a space where you can be honest. Nothing you say is going to shock me. So... what's brought you here today, from your perspective?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my work kind of made me come. There was an incident last week and HR said I had to do this or it goes in my file. So. [pause] I've been drinking more than I probably should, I guess. Wine, mostly. Every night since the baby came home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the wine has become a nightly thing — and part of you is already questioning whether that's okay.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It started as like, one glass after she went down for the night. Just to decompress, you know? But now it's... I don't know, half a bottle? Sometimes more. I'm just exhausted all the time and my brain won't turn off and it's the only thing that actually helps me sleep.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What does a typical evening actually look like for you right now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'm running on fumes by like six o'clock. Marcus does bath time because I just... I can't by then. And then she's finally down and I pour a glass and I sit there in the quiet and it's literally the only moment all day that feels like mine. And then I pour another one. And I keep thinking I should stop but I just... I don't even know if I can anymore. Like, what if I actually can't?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a really honest thing to say out loud — 'what if I can't.' A lot of people never get that far. And what I'm also hearing underneath all of it is someone who is completely depleted and just trying to make it through the day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I cry about it sometimes. Like, I'll be on my third glass and I'll look over at the monitor and I just feel... awful. She deserves better than this. Whatever this is. I don't even recognize myself right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about her. What's her name?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Lily. She's eight weeks. [small laugh] She already recognizes my voice, which is... I mean, that's amazing, right? And terrifying? Because I want her to see someone strong when she looks at me. Someone who has it together. Not someone who needs wine to get through the night. [voice catches] My mom was a drinker and I swore I would never — I'm not like her. But I don't want to be heading that direction either.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already know exactly what you don't want to pass down to her. That clarity — that love for Lily — that's not a small thing. That's actually one of the most powerful reasons for change I hear.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I never thought about it like that. Like it's not just about me being a mess — it's... she's going to be watching me. For years. Who I am is going to shape who she thinks she's allowed to be. God, I really don't want to screw this up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Can I reflect back what I'm hearing from you today? You came in because your job required it — but sitting here, it sounds like part of you has been waiting for a reason to look at this honestly. You're exhausted. You're grieving the version of yourself you thought you'd be as a mom. And at the same time, you are fiercely protective of Lily, and you already know the pattern you're determined not to repeat. That's not someone who doesn't care. That's someone who cares deeply and is just running out of road with the way things are now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I didn't expect to feel like someone actually gets it. [exhales] I think I do want to change. I just have no idea where to even start.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's exactly where we start — with not knowing. What would feel like one small, manageable step before we talk again? Just one.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe... telling Marcus. Like actually telling him how bad it's gotten. He knows I drink but I don't think he knows I'm scared about it. He'd want to help. He's good like that. That feels like something I could actually do.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey Marcus, good to meet you. I know doing this over video isn't always the most comfortable thing, so I appreciate you showing up today. There's no rush here. I'm just wondering — in your own words, what's kind of brought you to this point?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Look, I'm only here because my doc at the VA said I had to follow up after the ER thing. I don't... I mean, I don't think there's some big problem here. People go to the ER. It happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this felt like kind of an obligatory thing — showing up here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, pretty much. I mean, they said my levels were high or whatever. But I'd had a rough few days, hadn't eaten much. That stuff throws off your — you know, your blood work. It's not like I'm some... I'm not an alcoholic, if that's what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You want to make sure I'm not putting a label on you that doesn't fit. And I'm really not here to do that. I'm just — I'm curious about you, Marcus. What does drinking actually look like for you these days?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I have drinks at night to wind down. Most guys I served with do the same damn thing. When you've seen the stuff we've seen over there, you need something to take the edge off. That's just — that's just reality. Doesn't make me some kind of problem drinker.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Drinking became a way to manage some really heavy stuff you brought back from deployment. And you're not alone in that — a lot of vets have ended up in that same place. I'm wondering... is there any part of your life right now where it's started to create some friction? Anything sitting in the back of your mind?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... my wife. She's — she's been on my case about it. Said she'd leave if things didn't change. Which is... I don't know, that felt like an ultimatum and I don't really respond well to ultimatums. But she's... yeah. That's a thing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What she said landed differently than just noise. Even if it made you angry — some part of you is taking it seriously.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean — yeah. She doesn't say stuff like that lightly. She's put up with a lot. Late nights, me being checked out, the whole thing. We've got a daughter. She's seven. And I just... I don't want to be the guy who's not there, you know? My dad was like that and I swore I wouldn't be him.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's something really important — being present for your daughter, being a different kind of dad than you had. That matters deeply to you. It sounds like you've been carrying a lot, Marcus. The weight from deployment, trying to hold things together at home, and now feeling like things might be slipping in a direction you really don't want.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, when you put it like that... I don't know. I just figured I had it handled. And maybe I... maybe I don't. I haven't really let myself think about it that way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something to say that. What would things actually look like for you — if something shifted, six months from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... I'd want to actually be at dinner. Not just sitting there zoned out. Take my daughter to her soccer games without needing a drink first just to be calm enough to be around people. And, I don't know... maybe my wife would actually want to be in the same room as me again. That'd be something.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You can actually picture it. Being at that soccer game. Being at the table. And your wife choosing to be there with you. That's not a small thing to want — and it says a lot that it all comes back to the people you love.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean... I'm not saying I've got it all figured out. But, uh... maybe I'm willing to at least — I don't know, see what this looks like. I'm not making any promises. But... yeah. Maybe.

client_context: An 18-year-old referred by school counselor after being caught drinking at a school event. Feels singled out since 'literally everyone drinks'.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. I know walking into a place like this when you didn't exactly choose to be here... that's not always easy. So — what's your take on why you're here today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean, I didn't really have a choice, did I? My school counselor basically said I had to talk to someone or there'd be 'consequences.' So. I'm here. But honestly? It's ridiculous. I had like two sips of beer at a party and now suddenly I'm being treated like some kind of problem. Everyone was drinking. Literally everyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it feels completely unfair — like you got singled out for something everybody else was doing too.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes! Exactly. Like, why am I the one sitting in a counselor's office? Half my grade was at that party. Nobody else had to do this. I just... I don't think it's fair that I'm the one being made to feel like something's wrong with me when I literally didn't do anything different from anyone else. It's not like I was passed out on the floor or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me more about that night. What was going on for you before you decided to drink?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know, it was just... a normal thing? My friends were all doing it and I didn't want to be standing there with like, a water bottle looking like some kind of loser. You just go along with it. That's how it works. I'm not gonna be the one person who's like 'no thanks, I don't drink' while everyone else is having fun. That's not — that's not how friendships work.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Fitting in with your friends — that really matters to you. Not being on the outside.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. I mean, obviously. Doesn't it matter to everyone? I just didn't want to make it weird. It wasn't like I was even that into it — I don't even really like the taste. I just had some and I thought it was fine and then... I don't know. I didn't think it was gonna turn into all of this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Since all of this happened — what's been the hardest part for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My mom. She won't... she keeps saying she's 'disappointed,' which is so much worse than if she just yelled at me. She barely talks to me now. And I keep thinking like... do people think I'm, like, a bad person? Is that what this is? Because I'm not. I'm really not. I just wanted to have a normal night with my friends.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It really comes through how much you care about what the people close to you think of you — your mom, your friends. That's not a small thing. That's actually a lot of weight to be carrying.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I just... none of that went through my head in the moment. I just didn't want to feel left out. But now I'm like — what if this keeps happening? What if I keep doing things just because everyone else is and I keep hurting people who care about me and I don't even... I haven't really thought about it like that before, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you're in one of those moments — the pressure's on, everyone's doing it — what gets in the way of you being able to make a different call?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I don't know how to say no without it becoming this whole thing. Like people look at you, or they think you're judging them, or suddenly you're the weird one. And I hate that feeling. But I also just... I'm tired of situations like this. Like the aftermath. It's honestly exhausting and I didn't even — it wasn't even worth it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me make sure I'm understanding you right. You came in here today pretty sure this was all blown out of proportion — and maybe part of you still feels that way. And at the same time, somewhere in this conversation, something shifted a little. You're noticing that the cost of these moments — to your mom, to how you feel about yourself after — that's starting to add up. And there's a part of you that's wondering if you want something a little different going forward. Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah... yeah, I think so. I don't really know what that looks like or whatever. But... maybe there's something to actually think about here. I don't know. Maybe.

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again. Last time felt a little... unsettled when you left. How's the week been?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh god. Where do I even start. It was — okay so, my friend Maya basically turned my birthday dinner into like, an intervention. In front of everyone. My whole friend group just sitting there looking at me like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It was mortifying. And I just kept smiling because what else do you do, right? You just smile and get through it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your birthday. That's a really painful place for something like that to happen — people you love, and you're sitting there just trying to hold it together.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Eight years. Maya and I have been friends for eight years. And I kept replaying it all week, like, every night. And then Thursday I went out anyway because... I mean, what am I supposed to do, just sit at home and spiral? That's not who I am. Except I had more than I meant to, and I posted some stuff, and then my manager called Friday morning and just... *long pause* ...everything kind of collapsed at once. But it's fine. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What was it like to wake up Friday, before your manager called — that moment right when you first opened your eyes?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Awful. *laughs softly* Not that I'd admit that to literally anyone else. I felt like... I don't know, like something was sitting on my chest. And I looked at my phone and there were all these notifications and I just — I put it face down and stared at the ceiling for like twenty minutes. Which I never do. I'm always on my phone first thing. Content doesn't make itself, you know? But that morning I just... couldn't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes something real to say that out loud — that there was a morning you just couldn't. That's not a small thing to share.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... sure. I guess. *shifts* Look, I want to be clear — I'm not some cautionary tale. I have two hundred thousand followers who actually look to me for how to live well. Going out, brunches, events, that's literally my job. It's not the same as someone with a real problem. Maya just doesn't get the industry. My manager was overreacting. It was one post.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When you picture yourself a year from now — not the brand, not the platform — just you. What do you want that version of you to feel like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: That's... hm. *long pause* I mean, I want the collab to have launched. I want the numbers to be up. I... *trails off* I used to answer that question really easily, you know? Like, I always had this clear picture. And now when I try to see it I just get kind of... foggy. I don't know if that means anything. Probably just stressed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The picture used to be clear. Now it's foggy.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. *quiet for a moment* Don't — don't read too much into that. But yeah. Like I'll be at some event, somewhere I would have been so excited to be six months ago, and I just feel like I'm watching myself from outside. Going through the motions. And I wake up tired even when I slept. I haven't told anyone that. My whole thing is being the fun one, so. *small laugh* This is awkward to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it feel like to be genuinely excited again — not performing it, actually feeling it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. *exhales* That would be... that would be so good. I used to love my life. Like, actually love it, not just caption it. And I miss her — that version of me who was just, genuinely lit up about things. I'm not saying I have a drinking problem, I want to be super clear about that, that's not what this is. But maybe... I don't know. Maybe some things could shift a little. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So. A brutal week — your best friend's concern landed like a gut punch, Thursday got away from you, your manager called, and underneath all of it there's this woman who remembers what it felt like to be genuinely alive in her own life. And she came back here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. *pause* I didn't have to come back. I know that. *looks down, then up* I'm still not — I mean, I'm not ready to like, blow up my whole life or whatever everyone seems to want from me. But I came back. So. *small smile* I guess that's something, right?

client_context: A 33-year-old social media influencer whose entire social life revolves around drinking. Multiple friends have expressed concern. Insists it's just her lifestyle.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — I promise the couch is more comfortable than it looks. I'm Dr. Maya. So... first time here. How are you doing with all of this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um, yeah. I mean, I'm fine? Like, I don't really know why I'm here, honestly. My friends kept pushing me and then this thing happened and I was just like, okay fine, I'll go. But I want to be clear — I don't have a problem or anything. I'm just... I don't know. Being open-minded, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Open-minded — I'll take it. So something happened. What was the thing that actually made you pick up the phone and book this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay so — and this is mortifying, just so you know — I was at this brand collab event, like very on-camera, very important for my work, and apparently I was... not great. My manager called the next morning and goes, 'Sienna, we need to talk about your image.' Which, I mean. I'd had a few drinks but it was a long night and I hadn't eaten and literally everyone at these things drinks, that is the entire point. So I don't really think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you're in an industry where drinking is basically part of the job description, and then when something goes sideways, it's genuinely hard to separate that from the work itself.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly! Thank you. Like I have almost 800K followers and they follow me for a lifestyle — rooftop bars, wine launches, aperitivo hours in Milan. That's literally the content. So when my manager says 'image,' I honestly cannot tell if she means the drinking or if I wore the wrong shoes to a Chardonnay event, because I've done that too. It could go either way.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real bind. I want to ask about something you mentioned — your friends pushing you. What are they seeing that's got them worried?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... they think I drink too much. Which is a little rich given that they show up to all my parties and drink all my alcohol, so. But. There was this one night, my best friend Priya called me and she was actually crying. Like, not dramatic crying, just — quiet. She said she couldn't keep watching this. And I laughed it off in the moment, which... I probably shouldn't have done that. Because Priya isn't dramatic. She's really not. And she looked scared.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That one hit different. Someone you really trust — not a drama queen — and she was scared. That matters to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it does. I just... I don't recognize myself in the person she's describing, you know? Like when I look at my life I see someone who works insanely hard, who has this huge social presence, who knows how to have fun. I don't see whatever she's seeing. And that's... that's kind of the thing that's been sitting weirdly with me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That gap — between who you know yourself to be and what people you love are seeing — what's it like to actually sit with that for a second?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Scary. If I'm honest. Which I try not to be, about this specifically, because... what if they're right? Like I've built this whole persona, this whole brand, and what if underneath all of it I'm just — a drunk girl with good lighting? I've worked so hard. I don't want that to be the actual story. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, let me just hold up what I'm hearing for a second, because there's a lot here. You've built a life and a career around being magnetic, being present, being the person everyone wants to be around — and drinking has been so woven into that it's almost impossible to see where one ends and the other begins. But then there's Priya's face. And your manager's phone call. And whatever happened at that event that you haven't quite looked at directly yet. And somewhere underneath all of that, you came here today. Because something in you is a little scared, and maybe a little tired.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: God. When you line it up like that. I mean — I'm not going to like, fall apart right now, fair warning. And I'm still not totally sold on the whole 'I have a problem' framing. But... yeah. Okay. Maybe I'm more than a little scared. Is that something you can actually work with, or is this about to become a twelve-step thing with a lot of group feelings circles?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Ha — no feelings circles. I promise. And honestly, Sienna? You coming in here, half-convinced you don't need to be here, still a little scared? That's not nothing. That's actually one of the most real places anyone can start from.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, I can do real. Probably. Honesty is literally my brand, so. Let's just... see where this goes. No promises though.

client_context: A 32-year-old ER nurse who started drinking heavily during the pandemic. Feels guilty but says it's the only way to decompress after traumatic shifts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. Walk-in appointments can feel a little uncertain, so I want you to know there's no agenda here — we just talk. What brought you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor forwarded some labs. There was... the liver panel came back off. She said it wasn't an emergency but that I should, um, talk to someone. So here I am, I guess.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The lab results got your attention enough to come in, even though you weren't sure what to expect.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. But I want to be upfront — I work in the ER. I've been working in the ER through all of it, the pandemic, everything. My body has been through the wringer. Honestly it could be a hundred different things. I'm exhausted, I'm not sleeping well. I'm sure that's most of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: ER nursing through the pandemic — that's an enormous amount to carry. What does unwinding actually look like for you after a shift?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay, I drink. I know that's probably why I'm here. But it's not like — I'm not drinking at work, I'm not drinking in the morning. I come home, I have a few glasses of wine, sometimes more, and I can finally just... stop seeing everything I saw. It's the only thing that actually works. My brain just won't shut off otherwise.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You found something that gave you relief when nothing else did. That makes complete sense given what you're absorbing every single shift. You've been trying to survive this.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Thank you. Because people — my sister, whatever — they act like I'm some kind of... but they don't see what I see. I'm still showing up. I have a perfect attendance record. I'm doing my job.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're still showing up. That matters to you — being there for your patients. I want to ask you something and I hope it lands okay... has there been any moment recently at work where something felt off? Where you noticed yourself struggling in a way that surprised you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... yeah. Yeah, there was. Last Thursday. I missed a notation on a patient's chart — a med interaction. Nothing happened, we caught it, but my charge nurse pulled me aside and I just stood there and I couldn't even remember doing the assessment. Eight years. I have never — I've never had that happen. I told myself it was just a bad night but I've been thinking about it since.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That really shook you. Standing there and not being able to account for it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It scared me more than the labs did, honestly. Like the labs I could rationalize. But that? I pride myself on being sharp. On being the person other nurses come to. And lately I just feel like I'm... foggy. All the time. And I keep telling myself it's burnout but... I don't know. I'm not sure anymore where the burnout ends and the drinking starts.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: If things did start to shift — if you got some of that sharpness back — what would that mean for you? Not just at work, but for how you feel about yourself?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I'd feel like me again. The me that actually wanted to do this job, not just the me that's surviving it. I used to love nursing. I really did. I'd like to feel proud of a shift again instead of just relieved it's over.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, and you tell me if I've got it right. You came in today because of some lab results, but what's actually sitting with you is bigger than that — years of absorbing trauma in one of the hardest clinical environments there is, a coping strategy that gave you real relief when you needed it but that may now be getting in the way of the things you care about most: your patients, your sharpness, your sense of yourself as a nurse. And despite all of that, you walked in here today. That took something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I didn't really know how to put it together like that but. Yeah. I think I needed to hear someone say it out loud without making me feel like a disaster.

client_context: A 27-year-old bartender who drinks after every shift. Recently realized they can't remember the last sober day. Starting to question if this is normal.

utterances.speaker: therapist
