utterances.text: Good to see you again. I wasn't sure if you'd make it back, and... here you are. How've things been this past week?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Kind of pissed off about the whole thing. I kept thinking about what we talked about last time and it just — I don't know. It didn't sit right with me. Like, I left here feeling worse than when I came in.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something about last time stirred something up in you. Left you with this feeling that was hard to shake.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like — I work in a bar. Everyone around me drinks. My coworkers drink, my manager drinks, the regulars I've known for three years drink. So why am I the one sitting in some office talking about it? What does that say about me that I'm here and none of them are?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That's a real question. And you still came back. What made you decide to do that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I told myself I wasn't going to. I actually had my phone out Thursday to cancel. But then... something happened that night and I just kept thinking about it and I couldn't — I don't know. I couldn't let it go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something happened Thursday.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I got home and I couldn't remember the drive. Like, the whole drive. It's fifteen minutes, I do it every single night, there's nothing to it. And I was just... suddenly in my parking spot. I had to actually sit there and try to reconstruct it and there was nothing. Just a blank.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You arrived home and there was just... nothing there. A gap where the memory should be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, and that scared me, okay? I'll say it — that scared me. But I'm also not some... I function. I show up, I do my job, I'm not calling in sick, I'm not like falling apart. I just — I don't fit what I picture when I think of someone who has a problem with drinking.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It doesn't match the picture in your head of what that looks like. And at the same time — that blank on Thursday — when you really sit with it, what does it bring up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think about... it wasn't the first time. I've had other nights like that and I just kind of moved past them. And I keep telling myself nothing bad has happened, so it's fine. But... I don't know. Maybe I've just been lucky. Maybe that's all that is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It takes real courage to look at something like that and not just push it away. A lot of people would've cancelled Thursday and never thought about it again. You didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I'm here. That's something, I guess. I don't know what I want to do about any of it yet. But I keep thinking about my dad. He drank his whole life and he always said he was fine, everything was fine, and I swore I'd never be like that. And now I'm sitting here and I genuinely cannot tell you the last day I didn't drink anything. Not one day.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me just try to hold all of this together for a moment. You came back today, even when part of you was ready to walk away. Thursday night shook you in a way you couldn't ignore. And underneath all of it, there's something about your dad — and a promise you made yourself a long time ago about who you didn't want to become. You don't have answers yet. But there's a part of you that's starting to ask whether things are actually okay... or whether they aren't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. ... Yeah, that's pretty much it. I don't — I'm not ready to like, commit to anything. But that's it. That's what's going on.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for getting on the call. I know this wasn't exactly your idea. So — before we get into anything else — I want to hear it from you. What's your take on why you're here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My take? My take is HR completely overreacted to something that had nothing to do with my drinking. Some guy at work ran his mouth, I got loud, and somehow that turns into me sitting in front of a camera talking to a therapist. That's my take. I don't have a problem. I have a coworker who doesn't know when to shut up.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So the way you see it, this whole thing landed on you because of someone else's actions. You're here because of a chain reaction that started with him, not with you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And look — I'm not gonna sit here and pretend I'm some kind of... I don't know, alcoholic or whatever. I served two tours. I've seen things that would break most people. I handle my stuff. I have always handled my stuff. A few beers after work is not a crisis, no matter what anyone says.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Two tours is no small thing. And when you say you've always handled your stuff — I'm genuinely curious what that looks like. Walk me through a typical day when you get home from work.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... I come home, I decompress. I'll have a few beers, watch TV, whatever. That's it. That's what everybody I served with does — it's just how you wind down. My wife acts like I'm some kind of... I don't know. She doesn't get it. Nobody who wasn't over there gets it. It's fine. It's completely fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're still showing up. To work, to this call — even when you feel like none of it is necessary. That's not nothing. A lot of guys in your position would've just told HR to go to hell.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Yeah, I'm not gonna lose my job over this. I got bills. I got... yeah. It's just frustrating because I feel like everyone's treating me like I'm some kind of liability when I'm the same person I've always been. I just don't understand what changed. Or like, what everyone's so worried about all of a sudden.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned your wife a minute ago and then kind of moved past it. I don't want to let that go. What's actually going on there?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She... uh. She said she's done. Like — actually done this time. She's not dramatic, she doesn't say things she doesn't mean, so. I don't know. It felt different. She took the kids to her mom's last weekend and I came home to just... the house was empty. It was quiet in a way that didn't feel good.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: She took the kids. And something about the way she said it — or maybe just the empty house — made it feel more real than it has before.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. And I... look, I'm not ready to lose my family. I'm not. She went through both deployments with me, she dealt with me coming back the first time when I was... I wasn't easy. I know that. She stayed. She always stayed. And now she's at her mom's and I'm sitting here on a video call and I just — I don't know what I'd do if she actually left. Like, really left.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think there's more going on here than you came in with. You walked into this feeling like it was all a big misunderstanding — HR, the coworker, all of it. And some part of you still feels that way. But there's something underneath that: your wife, your kids, what you're actually at risk of losing. And the fact that she stayed through the hard stuff — that means something real to you. It's not a small thing that she's the one drawing the line now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No. No, it's not. I've seen guys back home — guys from my unit — who lost everything. Wives, kids, jobs. And I used to think, man, how do you let it get that far? How do you not see it coming? And now I'm sitting here and I'm like... I don't know. Maybe I haven't been seeing it. I swore I wasn't gonna be that guy.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You already have a clear picture of who you don't want to become. So tell me — what would the version of you that didn't lose everything actually look like?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know if I need to like... quit completely or whatever. I'm not saying that. But maybe... being more present when I'm home. My daughter — she's seven — she used to run to the door when I got home from work. Like, every single day. She stopped doing that. And I noticed. I noticed and I didn't... I didn't do anything about it. So. Yeah. Maybe that's where I start.

client_context: A 72-year-old with chronic pain who has been mixing alcohol with pain medication. Family is terrified. Doesn't want to burden anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Margaret, I really appreciate you coming in today, especially when I know you had to squeeze this between... what was it, a granddaughter's thing this afternoon? I won't keep you longer than we have. How are you doing right now, in this moment?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Oh, it's fine, I... yes, the recital is at four so I need to leave by three-fifteen at the latest. I'm fine. Honestly I wasn't sure what to expect coming here, Dr. Patel just said to come and talk to someone and I thought, well, alright. I'm not one to make a fuss.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Not one to make a fuss. That tells me something about you right there. Dr. Patel mentioned some things that came up at your last visit — but I'd rather hear it from you. What's been going on lately, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... the pain's been bad. The hip, and now it's the lower back too. And the medication helps, but it doesn't — it doesn't always take the edge off completely, you know? So sometimes in the evening I'll have a glass of wine. Maybe two. To help me sleep. I know he flagged that. I'm not... I'm not an alcoholic or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The pain is relentless, and you've found something that gives you a little relief in the evenings. And at the same time, there's a part of you that came in today — that sat down in that chair — which makes me think some piece of you has a question or two about it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yes. I suppose. My daughter, she found my — she saw the bottles in the recycling and she called me and she was just... she was crying, she was so upset. And I thought, it's wine, for goodness sake. But then I looked up the medication, the oxycodone, and what it said about mixing it and I got a little scared, I'll be honest with you.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You got scared. What did that feel like, reading that?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It felt... foolish. I felt foolish. I'm seventy-two years old, I've managed my whole life without anyone having to worry about me, and now my daughter is crying on the phone at ten o'clock at night and my son-in-law is sending me articles. They're scared and it's my fault and I just... I don't want to be someone people have to worry about. I never wanted that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've spent your whole life being the one who holds things together, not the one who worries people. And right now it feels like that's flipped. Like you've somehow become a burden. That's a painful thing to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It is. It really is. And I don't even — I mean, I'm not drinking to get drunk. I just want one night where I sleep more than three hours. The pain wakes me up and then I lie there and I think about my husband, he passed four years ago, and I think about whether my hip is going to get worse, and... the wine just quiets all of that down for a little while. That's all it is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's grief in there too. The pain, the sleeplessness, missing your husband — the wine has been doing a lot of work for you. And if I'm hearing you right, what you actually want is to sleep, to hurt less, and to not frighten your daughter. Those are the things that matter to you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's exactly right. I just... I never thought about it that way, that it's been doing all of that. I thought I was being practical. Sensible, even. But maybe I've been — I don't know. Maybe I've been managing everything on my own for so long that I didn't notice I was making a mess of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That kind of self-awareness — being able to see that clearly — that takes real courage, especially when it's not a comfortable thing to look at. And for what it's worth, you're not the first person sitting in that chair who was doing their very best with the tools they had. What I'm hearing is that you're open to finding better tools. Would it be alright if I shared a couple of things that sometimes help people in situations like yours?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Please. I — yes, I'd like that. I don't want my daughter crying over me. And honestly... I don't want to end up in the hospital because I was too stubborn to ask for help. My husband always said I was too stubborn. He wasn't wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just pull together what you've shared today, because you've covered a lot of ground in not very much time. You came in here not quite sure why, and you leave knowing that the wine has been helping you manage pain, grief, and sleeplessness all at once — and that it's also been scaring the people who love you, which matters deeply to you. You caught something in yourself today, Margaret. That's not nothing. I'd like to set up a follow-up and loop in Dr. Patel about some options for the sleep and the pain specifically. But — how are you feeling right now, before you head to that recital?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I feel... lighter, actually. Which I did not expect to say. I thought I'd come in here and feel judged and I don't. I feel like maybe there's something to be done about all of this. I'll call to make another appointment. I promise.

client_context: A 16-year-old whose parents found empty bottles hidden in their room. Brought to counseling against their will. Scared but trying to act tough.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, Marcus. Good to see you again. ... I heard this past week was a rough one. No pressure to dive into anything — I just want you to know I'm glad you came back in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't exactly have a choice. My parents literally sat in the car and watched me walk through the door. So. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're here because they made you come. That's a frustrating place to be — feeling like you don't have a say in something that's supposed to be about you.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... yeah. Like they're freaking out over nothing. A few beers, okay? Every kid does it. I don't know why it's such a massive deal. My dad drank when he was my age, I guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Mm. So part of what's hard is it feels like you're being singled out, or held to a standard that doesn't quite seem fair. ... And then on top of that, there was the stuff with your labs last week. I'm wondering — what was that like for you, getting those results?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Whatever. The doctor was probably being dramatic. They always do that, like, scare you so you'll do what they want. My liver thing — it's probably nothing. Lots of people have elevated... whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know the word they used. Elevated liver enzymes. ... You've been carrying that around all week, even if you're not sure what to do with it yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — okay, yeah, I looked it up. Online. But like, there's a million things that can cause that, it doesn't mean — I'm not some, like... I'm sixteen. That stuff happens to people who've been drinking for like thirty years, not me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You looked it up. ... What did you find, when you were reading about it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Stuff. Bad stuff, I guess. Like if you keep going it can turn into... I don't know. Things you can't fix. And I wasn't — I mean, I didn't think that was something I had to think about yet. I'm not even old enough to, like... it didn't seem like it applied to me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted when you saw that. Like... this wasn't supposed to be your problem yet, and now you're not so sure.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I drank again this week. After the results. I know that's... I know. I just — I didn't know what else to do with how scared I was. And then I felt worse after, and it was like, okay, that's... that's messed up, right? That I did that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Marcus, I want to reflect something back to you, because I think it matters. You got scary news. You did the thing you've been doing to cope. And then — instead of just letting it go — you sat with it, and you recognized something was off. That took honesty. Real honesty, the kind that's hard to come by at any age. ... You came back in today. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't — I'm not trying to, like, be some after-school special or whatever. But... I don't want my liver to be messed up at sixteen. That's not — that's not what I pictured. I kind of actually want to figure this out, maybe. I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't have to know how yet. That's what we're here for, together. ... If you could imagine yourself a few months from now — feeling less scared, maybe having a different way to deal with the hard stuff — what would that look like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Like... maybe just not hiding stuff all the time? It's exhausting, honestly. Having to remember where I put things, making sure my parents don't — it's a lot. I think I just want to not feel like I'm constantly about to get caught doing something.

client_context: A 21-year-old college senior who binge drinks every weekend. Friends staged an intervention but the student sees it as normal college behavior.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hey, come on in — grab a seat wherever feels comfortable. I'm Marcus. So it looks like today's a walk-in, which honestly, respect — that's not easy. What brought you through the door today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh... yeah. My friends basically forced me to come here. Like they staged this whole thing — I don't even know what to call it. An intervention? It was kind of humiliating, honestly. I sat there while they all like, read off a list. I don't think I actually need to be here.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So your friends went out of their way to set something up, and the whole thing felt more embarrassing than anything else.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Like... I get that they care or whatever, but it's — I don't know, it's just college. Everyone drinks. I party on weekends, that's it. I'm not some — I'm not an alcoholic sitting in a ditch somewhere. I just like to have fun. That's what being twenty-one is.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Yeah, fair enough — and I'm not going to argue with you about what's normal. I'm curious though, what do you think they actually saw? Like, what was it that got them worried enough to, you know, make a whole production out of it?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I... got a little out of hand a few times. But it's like — what am I supposed to do? Just not drink until I'm forty? Nothing's gonna change. Even if I wanted to, I live in a house with four guys and every weekend there's something. It's pointless to even think about.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You know what, you're being more real about those 'few times' than you actually had to be. A lot of people in your position would've just stared at the ceiling and said nothing. That's not nothing.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... there was this one night. A few weeks ago. I blacked out and apparently I — I don't really remember most of it. My roommate had to basically carry me home. And the next morning I felt like... not just hungover. Like actually kind of terrible. But that's one night, right? That doesn't make me some kind of problem person.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That morning after — what was actually going through your head when you were trying to piece together what happened?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was... scared, I think. Like, I couldn't remember full chunks of the night. And my roommate was just quiet about it, which is somehow worse than him being angry. I kept thinking — what if something had happened, you know? What if I'd gotten hurt or hurt someone. But then I just kind of... pushed it down. Because if I actually sit with it it just spirals and I can't do anything with that.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So there's already a part of you that knows something's off. You just haven't really let yourself stay in that feeling long enough to look at it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Maybe. I don't know. I don't want to like, blow it out of proportion either. But... yeah. I guess it's not nothing. My grades have been kind of in the toilet too and I keep telling myself it's the workload but — I mean, who studies hungover every single Monday? I don't know. I don't really like who I've been lately. That's weird to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Okay, so let me just kind of lay it back out — your friends staged an intervention, there was a night that scared you badly enough that you're still thinking about it weeks later, your grades are slipping, and you've got this quiet thing sitting in your chest that says you don't really like the version of yourself you've been lately. And at the same time, part of you is still saying 'I don't know if this is actually a real problem.' Both of those things are just... sitting there together.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's pretty much it. It's kind of a lot to hear all at once like that. I've been keeping all that stuff really separate in my head, I think. Like not letting them touch each other. Maybe... I don't know, maybe this isn't the worst idea. I still don't think I'm an alcoholic or whatever. But maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I'm not here to hand you a label — that's genuinely not what this is. But I'm curious. What would it even look like, even just a little bit, if things were different for you by the time you graduate in a few months?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I guess... like, actually making it to my Monday classes. Not dreading checking my phone the morning after a party. Not having to wonder what I did or said the night before. Not feeling like this. I don't know if any of that's actually possible at this point. But yeah. That would be — that'd be better.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in today. I know walking into a new place like this — especially when you weren't exactly looking to be here — isn't easy. I'd like to start by just hearing from you directly: what's your understanding of why you're here, in your own words?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor sent me. I didn't volunteer for this. He looked at some blood test and now apparently I need to sit in a counselor's office. No offense, but I've done this before — different place, different person — and it didn't do a damn thing for me. So.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So you've been through this before and walked away feeling like it was a waste of your time. That's worth knowing. And your doctor flagged something in those results that had him concerned enough to refer you — what did he actually tell you about what he found?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Said my liver enzymes are elevated. Which, I mean, I don't even know what that means exactly. But he's acting like I'm some kind of alcoholic. I have some beers after work — that's it. I work twelve-hour days in the sun, I'm swinging a hammer, I'm on my feet. You try doing that and tell me you don't want a drink when you get home.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hard physical work — you're exhausted, and unwinding at the end of the day feels like something you've earned.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. And now everyone's acting like I've got some — some big problem. My foreman drinks more than me. Half the guys on the crew drink more than me. I'm not missing work. I'm not stumbling around. I show up every single day, I do my job, I go home. So honestly? I'm kind of pissed off that I'm even sitting here right now.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're angry — and I want to say something: the fact that you showed up at all, feeling the way you do, that actually tells me something about you. A lot of people in your position just don't walk through the door.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I came because my wife asked me to. She's been on my case since the doctor called her. So fine, I figured, I'll go, I'll talk to whoever, and then everyone can calm down. Because I'm fine. That's — that's what I came here to say.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your wife's worried. Your doctor's worried. I hear that you think they're overreacting. But I'm curious about something — when the doctor first said the word 'liver,' in that moment, before the frustration kicked in... what went through your head?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... I don't know. My dad had liver problems. He died at sixty-one. So when the doctor said that — 'liver' — I kind of... I stopped listening to the rest of what he was saying. I just... yeah. But I'm not like my dad. I'm not. We're different people.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That word landed somewhere deep. Your dad, sixty-one — and you heard 'liver' and the room kind of went quiet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. He was only nineteen years older than me. And he drank — he wasn't... he didn't take care of himself. I always told myself I was different. But... okay, look, it's probably not just a beer or two. It's more like a six-pack. Most nights. I don't know, maybe more on weekends. I haven't really sat down and thought about it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I want to make sure I've got this right, because a lot has come out just now. You walked in here frustrated, feeling like this was all overblown. But underneath that there's your dad — gone at sixty-one, never met some of your kids. There's that moment in the doctor's office where you just went somewhere else when you heard 'liver.' And now, just in the last few minutes, you're telling me — maybe the amount is more than I've been saying out loud. That's a lot to be carrying into a room you didn't want to be in.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: When you put it all together like that... I don't know. I don't wanna be him. I don't wanna be sixty-one and — just gone. My youngest is seven. And I just... I don't even think about it anymore, the drinking. It's just what I do. End of the day, I get home, I crack one open, and then... I don't know. It's just what happens.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It's become automatic — not even a choice you're making anymore, just the routine. Given everything you just said, I want to ask you something, and I mean this genuinely: what do you want for yourself? Not what your wife wants, not what your doctor's pushing for. You.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to... I want to be around. For my kids. I don't want to be my dad. I don't know if I can do anything different — I really don't — but... maybe something's gotta change. I don't know what that looks like. But maybe.

client_context: A 24-year-old PhD student who has been drinking to manage thesis stress and imposter syndrome. Advisor noticed declining work quality.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Come on in, take a seat. I'm Marcus — most people just call me that, forget the title. Before we get into anything, I want you to know this stays here. Nothing goes back to your department, your advisor, none of that. This is just... your time. So, what brings you in today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Uh, yeah. So... my supervisor at the clinic — not my thesis advisor, the one at the part-time job — they filed some kind of report, and apparently that's what triggered this. I mean, I was there, I know what happened, I just... I'm not totally sure what I'm supposed to say here? Like, is this a evaluation thing, or...?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So it feels a bit murky — like you landed here but the why isn't fully clear to you yet.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Kind of, yeah. I mean, I get it — I showed up to a shift and I'd had a few drinks before, which I know was... look, it was a bad call. I'm not saying it wasn't. But it was one time. Mostly one time. I'm not like, stumbling around campus or anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Tell me about what life's been like lately — like, zoom out from that one shift. What's been going on?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... honestly it's been a lot. Third year of my PhD and the thesis is just — it's like I can picture exactly what it should look like and then I sit down and everything just disappears. My advisor's been dropping these comments about my output lately, which, I get it, he's not wrong, but... and I'm TAing, and doing the clinic hours, and I just — yeah. It's been a lot.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That gap — knowing exactly what you're capable of and then feeling completely blocked from it — that's one of the more exhausting places to sit.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that's... that's actually it exactly. And the drinking — it started as like, okay, one beer to take the edge off so I can actually sit down and write. And for a while it worked? Kind of. I'd relax enough to get something on the page. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What do you make of the 'kind of, maybe'?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... it stopped working. Like at some point I'd drink to write and I wasn't really writing, I was just — sitting there feeling less bad about not writing. And then I'd wake up feeling worse, and the chapter still wasn't done, so I'd need to... I don't know. Do it again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something that was supposed to be a bridge to your work started pulling you away from it instead.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: And that's what kills me. Because I actually — I care about this research. It's on long-term cognitive outcomes in veterans, longitudinal data, and I genuinely think it matters. Like, these are real people. And somewhere in the last... eight, nine months? I stopped feeling that. I just feel behind. Constantly behind.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So let me try to pull this together and see if I've got it right. You're here because of a serious incident at work — one you're not minimizing. But underneath that, there's this bigger picture: a PhD student who genuinely cares about work that matters, research on veterans, who got absolutely buried under the pressure of year three and found something that seemed to soften the edges. And now that thing is costing more than it gives. And somewhere along the way, you lost the thread back to why you started this in the first place.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. When you lay it out like that. I haven't actually said any of this out loud before. To anyone.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean for you — and for that research — if you could get some of that back? That sense of why you're doing this?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I think... I think I'd actually finish it. I think I'd be good at this again. I used to be good at this — like, I didn't get into this program by accident. I don't know exactly when I stopped believing that, but I think if I could clear some of the noise... yeah. I think I could get back there.

client_context: A 36-year-old veteran who started heavy drinking after deployment. Views drinking as normal military culture. Wife threatened divorce.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you again, Marcus. You mentioned when you called that things have been a little rough lately. Tell me where things are at for you right now.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it's whatever. Had a couple rough nights, that's all. Everybody has rough nights. Doesn't mean there's some big crisis or whatever.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A couple rough nights, and you're not convinced that means anything bigger is going on.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Right. Yeah. I just... look, I've been mostly keeping it together. Week before last was actually pretty decent. I didn't — I mean it wasn't perfect but it was better than before. And then... I don't know. It just kind of fell apart a little. That happens to everybody.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When things fell apart — what was that actually like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Same as always, I guess. You hit a wall, you deal with it. That's just how it goes. I don't see what talking about it is gonna change. I've been through worse. Way worse. This is nothing.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've pushed through a lot — that's real. And you still showed up here today, even when part of you figured it wouldn't make a difference. That takes something.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ... Yeah. I don't know. Sandra — my wife — she, uh... she called me out this weekend. Said I smelled like booze at Jake's soccer game. I didn't even... I thought I was okay. I thought I had it handled.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That moment — Jake on the field, Sandra saying that to you — what was going through your mind right then?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I was... embarrassed. Which, you know, I don't — I don't get embarrassed easy. But standing there with all those other parents, and he's running around on the field, and she's looking at me like... like I'm some kind of... I don't know. I felt like garbage. Like I let him down. Both of them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Jake and Sandra matter to you. Deeply. And what happened at that game — it cut through in a way that the rough nights alone haven't.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I didn't come home from two tours to be that guy, you know? My dad was that guy. I swore I wasn't gonna be him. And here I am and... I mean, maybe — maybe there's still a version of this where I actually fix it. I don't know. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me pull together what I'm hearing. You came in today feeling like nothing was going to shift — like this is just how it goes. And then you brought up the soccer game, Sandra, Jake. And something changed in the room just now. You're thinking about your dad, about the man you decided you were going to be when you enlisted. And there's still a part of you that believes he's still possible. That part didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it is. I just... I need to figure out how to do this without feeling like I'm starting over from zero every single time. But yeah. That part's still there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Given everything you just said — what would one small thing look like this week? Something that's yours. Not Sandra's ask. Not mine.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? Just... not drinking before Jake's practices. That's it. That's the one place I — I don't want to be that guy there. Start with that.

client_context: A 48-year-old who has been drinking heavily since his divorce 4 months ago. Alternates between anger at his ex and sadness about losing his family.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you made it in today. Last week sounded rough. Tell me what's been going on since you left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... it wasn't some big crisis or whatever. My neighbor overreacted, called 911. Blood pressure was up, they kept me overnight, ran a bunch of tests. I'm fine. It was embarrassing more than anything.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Your neighbor was worried enough to call for help. What was going on that night that got you to that point?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Sarah's lawyer sent — there was paperwork about the house. About the sale. And I just... I'd been drinking since, I don't know, noon maybe. Started throwing stuff around the apartment. I don't remember all of it, honestly. I remember the paramedics being there and thinking, how did this happen. I don't do that. That's not me.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: When that paperwork landed, something just shut off in you. Like the floor dropped out.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, kind of. I keep thinking I'm doing okay, like I've got it under control, and then something like that hits and I just — I scared myself a little. I'm not going to lie. Waking up in the ER and not fully knowing how you got there... that's not a good feeling.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That took something to say — that you scared yourself. A lot of people wouldn't go there. What does it mean to you that you reacted that way?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It means... god. I don't know. It means I don't recognize myself. I had a life. We had a house, I coached my son's baseball team, I saw my kids every single day. Now I'm in some apartment and I get them every other weekend and... I miss them. I really miss them. I didn't think it would feel like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: The drinking isn't really about Sarah, or the paperwork. It's about not knowing what to do with that much loss.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I keep telling myself I'm angry at her, and... I am. I am angry. But underneath that, if I'm honest... I just want my family back. And I can't have that. So I don't know what to do with that. The drinking just — it makes everything quiet for a while. A few hours where I don't have to think about any of it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me try to pull this together. You came in today after a really frightening night — one you didn't plan to have. Under all the anger at Sarah, there's this enormous grief about losing your kids, your home, your daily life. For months, drinking has been the only thing that's made that quiet. But last week, it stopped feeling manageable. It started feeling dangerous. Does that track?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...yeah. Yeah, that's — that's right. I haven't heard it laid out like that before. It sounds worse when you say it out loud.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: On the weekends you have your kids — what kind of father do you want to be for them?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I want to be present. Actually there, not just in the room. My dad was a drinker. And even when he showed up, he wasn't really... there. I swore I'd never be that. And now I'm — I'm turning into him. My son is twelve. He notices things. I don't want him to remember me the way I remember my dad. I don't.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You've been carrying that promise to yourself for a long time — that you wouldn't repeat what you grew up with. That's still in you. That hasn't gone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I know. I know it hasn't. I just — I think I need to actually do something. Not just come in and talk, not just white-knuckle through the week. Actually do something different. Maybe... can we talk about what that looks like? Like, concretely? Because I'm tired. I'm really tired of feeling like this.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So, rough night, huh? Come on in, grab a seat — I'm Mike, one of the counselors here. I know the ER isn't exactly the Ritz Carlton. I appreciate you sticking around to talk instead of just walking out, which, let's be honest, a lot of guys do. What's your sense of why they sent you over to see me?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Hell if I know. I had a few drinks, maybe more than I should've, and next thing there's some twenty-something doctor telling me I need to talk to somebody. I don't need a shrink. I was fine.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You were fine — and having some kid half your age tell you otherwise felt like a bit much.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I spent thirty years in the Army. Thirty. I've been through things that would make that doctor's head spin. And now I can't have a couple drinks in my own house without it being some kind of... emergency? Come on. That's insulting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thirty years — that's not a small thing. That's a whole identity, a structure, a purpose, people counting on you every single day. And then one day it's just... over. What's the retirement piece actually been like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's... fine. I thought I'd enjoy it, you know? Golf, fishing, whatever. But it's quieter than I figured on. My wife passed three years back. Kids are out in Phoenix and Denver. So it's... yeah. It gets quiet.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: A lot of quiet. And the drinking kind of... fills some of that.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean — maybe. Sure. But it's not like I'm stumbling around the house. I have a few after dinner, sometimes more if I can't sleep. It helps. And I'm not some... I'm not a drunk, if that's what you're writing over there.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me make sure I'm getting this right, and stop me if I'm off. You've had this enormous life — three decades of service, a marriage, raising a family. And now it's just you in a quiet house, and the drinking isn't a problem from where you sit, it's more like it's doing something for you, helping you get through the nights. But then there's the liver thing your doctor flagged, and last night. When you look at all of that together... what does it bring up?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... huh. I don't know. The liver thing — that scared me, if I'm being honest. My buddy Frank had liver problems. He went fast. Real fast. And he was my age.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Losing Frank that way hit close to home.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, it did. He probably didn't think it would get that bad either. And I keep thinking... my kids already lost their mother. I don't want them getting a call like that about me. Not like that. I've already missed so much with them, all those deployments.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What would it mean — to you, to them — if things looked different a year from now?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I'd... I'd like to actually be around. I got a granddaughter who just started walking. I want to see more of that. I've already missed enough. I don't want to miss the rest of it because I was sitting alone drinking in the dark, you know?

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So here's what I'm hearing — tell me if I'm off. You're a man who gave a lot, for a long time, to a lot of people. And somewhere in the quiet of retirement, drinking crept in and started doing a job for you. You don't see yourself as someone with a problem — and honestly, that makes complete sense, because that's not how it feels from the inside. But there's also a part of you that's thinking about Frank, thinking about your liver, thinking about a little girl who just learned to walk. And that part is starting to wonder if something needs to change. Not because some ER doc said so. Because you want to be there.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, that... that lands. I don't even know what changing it looks like, or how you fill the time otherwise. But... yeah. Maybe I should actually talk to somebody about all of it. For real. Not just because they told me to.

client_context: A 26-year-old software engineer with severe social anxiety who uses alcohol as liquid courage at every social event. Knows it's a crutch but terrified of life without it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Hi, I'm really glad you came in today. I know this might not have been, um, the appointment you were looking forward to. How are you feeling about being here?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Honestly? I'm kind of pissed off. Like, my company basically forced me to come here. I don't even... I mean, I made one mistake at the holiday party. One. And now I'm being treated like I'm some kind of... I don't know. It's humiliating. I finished the detox, I did everything they asked.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: It sounds like this whole situation has felt really unfair. Like one moment got turned into something much bigger than you think it deserved.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Because it's not like I'm some... I'm not an alcoholic, okay? I get really nervous at work events, always have, and I just had a little too much and said something embarrassing to my VP and it became this whole thing. Meanwhile there were like six other people just as drunk as me and nobody said anything to them.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You mentioned getting really nervous at work events. I'm curious — what does that nervousness feel like for you, like right before you walk in the door?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: It's awful. My heart races, I can't think straight, I say the wrong things or I just freeze up completely. Everyone's doing the small talk thing and I'm standing there like... like a statue. It's been like that my whole life, it's not just work stuff. I've always been like this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this anxiety isn't new — you've been carrying it for a really long time. And somewhere along the way you found that drinking... quieted it down. Made things feel more manageable.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. It's like... it was the only thing that ever worked. One or two drinks and I could actually talk to people. I felt like a normal person. And I know — I know how that sounds. I'm not stupid. I know it's not a solution. But I genuinely don't know what else to do and that's... that's honestly the scariest part of all this.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That fear of not knowing what else to do — I want to stay with that for a moment. What does it look like to you, the idea of showing up to a social situation without that... safety net?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Terrifying. Like... I had a full panic attack at a wedding two years ago. Before I started drinking regularly. I had to leave, I sat in my car for an hour, I just... I can't go back to that. I can't. But I also can't keep doing this either. The detox was horrible. I don't ever want to do that again.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're holding something really heavy right now. The fear of going back to that panic, and at the same time knowing that the way you've been coping isn't working anymore. And you're still here. That takes real courage, honestly.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... yeah. I never really thought about it that way. I've just been so ashamed, you know? Like, I'm a software engineer, I'm supposed to have my life together, and here I am because I got drunk at the company Christmas party and embarrassed myself in front of everyone. It's just... ugh.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: I really hear the shame in that, and I want us to come back to it. But I'm wondering — when you imagine a version of yourself who has found a different way to handle the anxiety... what does she look like? What's she doing?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Um... that's kind of a weird question but... I guess she's still a little awkward? Like, that's probably just who I am. But maybe she's okay with it. She has, like, actual tools or something. Which is funny because I've never actually tried therapy for the anxiety. Or medication. I just kind of... self-medicated, I guess. Figured it out on my own. Badly.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me just reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You came in today angry, and that makes complete sense — this wasn't your choice. But underneath that there's this anxiety that's been with you a really long time and has never actually been treated. You found something that worked until it stopped working. You're scared of going back to the panic, and you're clear you don't want to go through detox again. And somewhere in this conversation, you started imagining a version of yourself with real tools. That shift — that feels really significant.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I... I actually want to figure this out. Not just because my job is on the line. Like, genuinely. I'm so tired of being scared all the time. That's not... that's not a way to live.

client_context: A 42-year-old construction worker who drinks a six-pack every night. Referred by his doctor after abnormal liver tests. Thinks the doctor is overreacting.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Thanks for coming in. So... tell me, what made you decide to walk through that door today?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: My doctor. She's making a whole big thing out of nothing. I had some bloodwork come back a little off and now suddenly I need — I don't know, counseling or whatever. I'm only here 'cause she wouldn't let it go.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So this feels like it was forced on you. Like coming here wasn't really your idea.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: No offense but yeah. Look, I do construction. Twelve-hour days sometimes, in the summer heat, hauling materials. A six-pack at the end of the day is just — that's normal. That's what guys do. She's acting like I'm some kind of... like I got a problem. I don't have a problem.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: That label — having a problem — that really doesn't fit for you. You've got a job, a life, you show up every single day.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Exactly. Twenty years I've been doing this. I don't miss work, I don't drive drunk, I'm not some guy passed out on the floor. I don't know why nobody can see that. It's like the second the doctor sees a number she doesn't like, suddenly everything I do is wrong.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Twenty years of showing up, of building things... and then a piece of paper comes back with some numbers and suddenly it's like the ground shifts a little. I'm wondering what that was like — getting those results.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I mean... look. My dad had liver problems. He died at 58. So yeah, okay, the liver thing, that kinda — it stuck with me a little. But she said it's early, like it could go either way. I just don't need people piling on top of me about it, you know? I already feel like garbage.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text:
... Your dad. Fifty-eight. 

That sits with me.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, he drank way more than me. Way more. I'm not like him. But... I don't know. I'm 42. He was 42 once.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Something shifted when those results came back. Even a little. You don't have to call it anything — but part of you came in here today.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I... okay, yeah. I cut back for like two weeks after she told me and I felt — I don't know, better? Like I actually slept. But then work got rough again and it just crept back up and — I'm not gonna apologize for how I unwind. It's a hard job.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You don't owe me or anyone an apology. But I'm curious about those two weeks — you said you felt better. What did better feel like for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Slept better. My back hurt less in the mornings, which sounds stupid but — and my wife, she didn't say anything but she was just... I don't know. Nicer? Like there was less tension in the house. I noticed it.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So without a single word between you, she noticed something. And you noticed something in yourself — the sleep, the pain, the feeling in your own house. That's not nothing. For a guy who says he came in here just because his doctor wouldn't stop... that's actually a lot to sit with.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text:
... Yeah. 

I guess it's not nothing. I just don't — I don't know what I'm supposed to do with any of this.

client_context: A 65-year-old retiree who started drinking more since retirement due to loneliness and loss of purpose. Doctor flagged liver concerns at last checkup.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Good to see you, Harold. I know it's been a tough week. When you called to reschedule, you mentioned things got pretty rough — I'd like to hear from you what happened, if you're willing to walk me through it.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah, I... ended up in the ER Friday night. My son — he lives about an hour away — he called to check in and I guess I wasn't... sounding right to him. He drove up, took one look at me and drove me straight there. They kept me overnight. Blood pressure, they said. And some other numbers were off. I'm fine though. It was... it was a lot of fuss over nothing, really.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: So on one hand, you're grateful your son was there — and on the other, it feels like everyone's making more of this than it needs to be.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Well... yeah. I mean, I know I've been drinking more than I should. I'm not stupid. But I had a bad week, okay? Margaret's birthday was Thursday — that's my wife, she passed four years ago — and I just... I don't know. I don't need people treating me like I'm some kind of... I handled myself fine for sixty-five years.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Margaret's birthday. That's a heavy day to carry alone. What was that like for you this year?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: What do you think it was like? I sat in that house by myself, same as every year since she's been gone. Same four walls. I don't — look, I don't need to relive it. I drank. It got out of hand. That's it. That's the whole story. I don't see why we need to make it into some big... analysis.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You're not here to be analyzed. You want someone to understand that you were in real pain — and that reaching for something familiar made sense in that moment.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: ...Yeah. Yeah, that's — yeah. I just. I wasn't trying to end up in some hospital. I wasn't trying to scare my boy. That's not — that's not what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: You care deeply about your son. That comes through clearly. And you're sitting here today — the day after being discharged — which tells me something about who you are. Even when things fall apart, you still show up.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: He was... he was pretty shaken up when he saw me. Didn't say much but I could tell. He's got his own family now, grandkids — he doesn't need to be driving an hour at ten at night because of me. I don't want to be a burden to him. And the doctor at the hospital, she said some things about my liver that I didn't... I didn't really want to hear.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: What did she say that stuck with you the most?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: She said if I keep this up I'm looking at serious damage. Cirrhosis, maybe. She wasn't mean about it, just very... direct. And I kept thinking about my brother. He died at sixty-eight. Different reasons but still. I'm sixty-five. I sat with that number all weekend.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: Let me reflect back what I'm hearing, because I think it matters. You had a devastating week — Margaret's anniversary, the ER, a hard conversation with a doctor, watching your son worry about you. And underneath all of that, there's something you're starting to sit with — that the path you're on has real costs. For your body, for your son, maybe even for how much time you have. When you hold all of that together, what comes up for you?

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: I don't want to die like this. Alone in that house, just... drinking myself into nothing. That's not — that's not who I am. I was a good father. I worked hard. I had a life. I just, somewhere after Margaret, I kind of... stopped. And I think I've been telling myself it doesn't matter, that nobody would notice anyway. But my son noticed. He drove an hour at ten o'clock at night. He noticed.

utterances.speaker: therapist
utterances.text: He noticed. And somewhere in you — even through all the grief and the loneliness — you noticed too. That's why you kept your appointments even when things got hard. That's why you're here today, the day after being discharged, instead of being back in that house. You said you don't want to die like this. That's not a small thing. That sounds like something worth building on.

utterances.speaker: client
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah, I think... I think I'm ready to actually try. Not just show up and talk about it. Actually try. I don't know exactly what that looks like yet, but... I'm tired of fighting it. I'm just tired of feeling like this.
